questions.worked_solution:
Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** We are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=7\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 11 & -4 \\ -1 & -10 & 3 \\ -1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -11 & -4 \\ 1 & -10 & -3 \\ -1 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ -11 & -10 & 3 \\ -4 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ -11 & -10 & 3 \\ -4 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
given that $det(A)=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** We are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A$ $=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ if its determinant is $-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3-0) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21}=\frac{1}{-2}\cdot (-3)=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|-(-2)|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|+4|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(6-0)+2(0+1)+4(0+3) \\  & =6+2+12 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-4-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21}=\frac{1}{20}\cdot 4=\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

The entry ${a}_{23}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & k & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

equals $-1.$ Find the value of $k.$

$k=${{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & k & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ k & -2\end{aligned}|-(-1)|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 3 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(1\cdot (-2)-(-1)\cdot k)+(0\cdot (-2)-(-1)\cdot 3)+(0\cdot k-1\cdot 3) \\  & =2(k-2)+3-3 \\  & =2k-4\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{23}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{23}^{t}={c}_{32}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{32} & =(-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(2\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 0) \\  & =-(-2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{23}^{′} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{c}_{23}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{c}_{32} \\  & =\frac{2}{2k-4} \\  & =\frac{1}{k-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{23}^{′}=-1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{k-2} & =-1 \\ 1 & =-(k-2) \\ k-2 & =-1 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(4-2) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}^{t}={c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(1\cdot k-0\cdot 1) \\  & =-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{(1-2k)}\cdot (-k) \\  & =\frac{k}{\,2k-1\,}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{12}^{′}=\frac{1}{3}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{\,2k-1\,} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ 3k & =2k-1 \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inverse of a 3x3 Matrix Using the Matrix of Cofactors
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 4 & -3 & 8\end{aligned}| & =0|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 8\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-(8-12)+2(-3-0) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 8\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 8\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 & -3 \\ 14 & -8 & -4 \\ 3 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
[\begin{aligned}9 & -(-4) & -3 \\ -(14) & -8 & -(-4) \\ 3 & -(-2) & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
[\begin{aligned}9 & -14 & 3 \\ 4 & -8 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -14 & 3 \\ 4 & -8 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -14 & 3 \\ 4 & -8 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{9}{2} & 7 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & -1 \\ \frac{3}{2} & -2 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Determine the entry $a'_{23}$ in the inverse of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =-2|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-3)|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(2-0)-3(0-0)-3(0-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry $a'_{23}$ in $A^{-1},$ we need to know the value of $c_{32}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{32} & =(-1)^{3+2}{M}_{32} \\  & =(-1)^{5}|\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1\cdot (0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det (A)}C^{T},$ we have

$$
a'_{23} = \dfrac{1}{-1}c_{32} = -1\cdot 0 = 0.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Cofactor Method To Solve for an Unknown Quantity
canonical_examples.problem:
The entry $a'_{31}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & k & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]$ 
equals $1$. Find the value of $k$.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & k & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =3|\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-2)|\begin{aligned}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(3k-0)-2(-6-0)-2(6+k) \\  & =9k+12-12-2k \\  & =7k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry $a'_{31}$ in $A^{-1},$ we need to know the value of $c_{13}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{13} & =(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =6+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det (A)}C^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13} \\  & =\frac{1}{7k}\cdot (6+k) \\  & =\frac{6+k}{7k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that $a'_{31}=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6+k}{7k} & =1 \\ 6+k & =7k \\ 6 & =6k \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
